name: Dr. C.H. Berry's Freckle Ointment

card.summary: An early-1900s Chicago freckle cream, sold in a white glass jar, that aimed to lighten freckles and blotchy skin for a clearer complexion.
card.note: Contained ammoniated mercury, a toxic ingredient used in historic skin lighteners.

quick.overview:
Dr. C.H. Berry's Freckle Ointment was a mass-market cream sold from the early 1900s, advertised to remove freckles, tan, moth patches and other skin discolourations for a clearer complexion.

Its active ingredient was ammoniated mercury, a skin-bleaching agent common in such products, which is the reason it is remembered as a historical case of mercury skin lighteners.
quick.how: It was applied as an ointment sold in a white opal glass jar through mail-order catalogues such as Sears, Roebuck, in cosmetics sections.
quick.risks: Ammoniated mercury is toxic. Reported contents ranged from about 5% to 12% in different analyses, and a 1912 injunction was issued against the product.

lead: Dr. C.H. Berry's Freckle Ointment was a freckle and skin-bleaching cream sold by the Dr. C.H. Berry Company of Chicago. It was advertised for freckles, tan, moth patches, pimples, eczema and muddy complexion, aiming at an even, lighter skin tone.[1]

Its active ingredient was ammoniated mercury; published reports gave mercury content of 9.8% in a 1930 North Dakota bulletin and 12% in a 1912 Good Housekeeping article, while a laboratory test of one jar found 5.4%.[1]
Sears catalogues sold it in a distinctive jar from 1908 to at least 1933.[1]

angle.text: It was used to lighten freckles and discolourations through ammoniated mercury, which bleaches pigment.

infobox: 1908 to at least 1933 in this jar style[1]

paras: The company originally styled itself the Dr. C.H. Berry Chemical Company and presented itself as a patent medicine producer, with the name taken from a Chicago specialist of the late 1800s; it became linked to women's cosmetics later.[1] A 1912 injunction against the product is shown in the source, though its terms are not described.[1]
Government agencies and professionals criticised mercury in such products because of toxicity, yet the ointments stayed popular with women.[1]

timeline.event: Jar style listed in Sears catalogues.[1]
Injunction against the product; Good Housekeeping reports 12% mercury.[1]
